claim: Vocal development is the adaptive coordination of the vocal apparatus, muscles, the nervous system, and social interaction.
source: Vocal development is the adaptive coordination of the vocal apparatus, muscles, the nervous system, and social interaction.
evidence: This is a definitional statement presented in the abstract that frames the study's conceptual approach.

claim: Only the combination of the developing vocal tract, vocal apparatus muscles and nervous system can fully account for the patterns of vocal development in marmoset monkeys.
source: With a biomechanical model of the marmoset monkey vocal apparatus and behavioral developmental data, we show that only the combination of the developing vocal tract, vocal apparatus muscles and nervous system can fully account for the patterns of vocal development.
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results presented throughout the manuscript showing that each element alone is insufficient.

claim: Infant marmosets produce mostly immature calls (cries and subharmonics) during early postnatal days which are replaced by more adult-like calls (phees) during development.
source: Infant marmosets produce mostly immature calls (cries and subharmonics) during early postnatal days which are replaced by more adult-like calls (phees) during development.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and shown in Figure 1b with spectrograms of different call types.

claim: The dominant frequency of marmoset infant vocalizations decreases during development.
source: Changes in vocal acoustics during development include a lowering of the dominant frequency. Purple curve shows a cubic spline fit to the data.
evidence: Figure 1c shows data points and a fitted curve demonstrating the decrease in dominant frequency over postnatal days.

claim: The probability of parental contingent responses is negatively correlated with the zero-crossing day in marmoset vocal development.
source: Relationship between the probability of parental contingent responses and the zero-crossing day. Purple line shows the linear regression fit to the data.
evidence: Figure 1e shows a negative linear relationship between these variables with a regression line.

claim: Young swamp sparrows cannot imitate artificially sped up versions of their species' song, demonstrating muscular constraints on learning.
source: For example, young swamp sparrows cannot imitate artificially sped up versions of their species' song, demonstrating muscular constraints on learning (Podos, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Podos, 1996.

claim: In human infants there is growth in the vocal apparatus during development.
source: Along similar lines, in human infants there is not only growth in the vocal apparatus (Fitch and Giedd, 1999; Vorperian et al., 2005), but developmental changes in vocalization-related motor control (Green et al., 2000) and respiration (Boliek et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fitch and Giedd, 1999 and Vorperian et al., 2005.

claim: In songbirds, bats, marmoset monkeys and humans, social responses by adults influence vocal development.
source: Moreover, in songbirds (West and King, 1988; Chen et al., 2016), bats (Prat et al., 2015), marmoset monkeys (Takahashi et al., 2015; Gultekin and Hage, 2017) and humans (Kuhl et al., 2003; Goldstein et al., 2003; Goldstein and Schwade, 2008), social responses by adults influence vocal development.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations across different species.

claim: Waddington envisioned cellular differentiation as a ball rolling down a surface with hills and valleys in an epigenetic landscape.
source: Waddington (Waddington, 1957) envisioned this canalized pattern as a ball (the cell's state) rolling down a surface with hills and valleys to seek the lowest points in an epigenetic landscape.
evidence: This is a description of Waddington's metaphor supported by citation to Waddington, 1957.

claim: The Waddington landscape metaphor for cellular development was given a formal quantitative theoretical framework by Wang et al., 2011.
source: Recently, this metaphor for cellular development was given a formal quantitative theoretical framework (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2011.

claim: Marmoset monkey vocal development shares numerous parallels with prelinguistic vocal development in humans.
source: Moreover, we are gaining knowledge of the genetics of this species (Harris et al., 2014) and, more specifically, the sensorimotor physiology related to its vocal production (Eliades and Wang, 2008; Miller et al., 2015; Zhang and Ghazanfar, 2016; Borjon et al., 2016; Roy et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations and is stated in the context of justifying marmosets as a model.

claim: The biomechanical model used in this study is based on a second order ordinary differential equation with two time-varying parameters: α(t) representing air pressure and β(t) representing vocal fold tension.
source: Briefly, we use a model that is a second order ordinary differential equation with two possible time-varying parameters: α⁢(t), representing the air pressure produced by the lungs and β⁢(t), representing vocal fold tension (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 3a.

claim: Vocal amplitude is mainly controlled by air pressure.
source: Vocal amplitude is mainly controlled by the air pressure (Sundberg et al., 1993), which the model expresses as nearly vertical iso-amplitude (same amplitude) curves in Figure 3h.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sundberg et al., 1993 and demonstrated in Figure 3h.

claim: The increase in vocal tract length L and the associated changes in resonance frequencies during development can explain the observed reduction in the dominant frequency of vocalizations.
source: As expected, the increase in L and the associated changes in resonance frequencies during development can explain the observed reduction in the dominant frequency of vocalizations.
evidence: This is stated after fitting the model to the developmental data on dominant frequency changes.

claim: Laryngeal and respiratory muscle size, strength, and dynamics significantly change through postnatal development in humans.
source: Laryngeal and respiratory muscle size, strength, and dynamics significantly change through postnatal development in humans (Moore, 2004; Sasaki, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Moore, 2004 and Sasaki, 2006.

claim: The larger proportion of cries in the early postnatal period is due to very young infants having difficulty producing higher air pressures and vocal fold tensions required to generate mature (phee) calls.
source: Based on this assumption, one possibility is that the larger proportion of cries that occurs in the early postnatal period is due to very young infants having difficulty producing higher air pressures and vocal fold tensions required to generate mature (phee) calls (Figure 3f).
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the text and supported by the parameter mapping in Figure 3f.

claim: A two-element developmental landscape that includes vocal tract growth and the development of muscle control can account for lowering of the dominant frequency and the rapid transition from early immature calls to mature ones.
source: Thus, a two-element developmental landscape that includes vocal tract growth and the development of muscle control of the vocal apparatus can account for two key features of vocal development: lowering of the dominant frequency as calls become more mature and the rapid transition from early immature calls to mature ones.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the modeling results presented in Figure 5.

claim: The cost function that only includes vocal tract growth and muscular control improvements cannot explain the correlation between parental feedback and the rate of the cry-to-phee transition.
source: We observe that there are clear correlations between the amount of parental feedback and the rate of the cry-to-phee transition (Figure 5f, purple line) but these cannot be explained by the cost function that only includes the elements of vocal tract growth and muscular control improvements (Figure 5f, gray line).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing the data (purple line) with model predictions (gray line) in Figure 5f.

claim: Contingent parental responses are those that are produced within 5 s of an infant call.
source: Contingent parental responses are those that are produced within 5 s of an infant call.
evidence: This is a methodological definition stated in the text.

claim: Infants that receive a higher proportion of contingent parental calls exhibit earlier transitions from cries to phees.
source: Infants that receive a higher proportion of contingent parental calls exhibit earlier transitions from cries to phees.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by the correlation shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Infant marmoset calls that are more tonal (or 'phee' like) are more likely to elicit parental responses.
source: However, infant marmoset calls that are more tonal (or 'phee' like; [Figure 1b, right panel]) are more likely to elicit parental responses (Takahashi et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Takahashi et al., 2016.

claim: The relationship between the proportion of contingent parental calls and the zero-crossing day can be explained by the development of the nervous system facilitated by parental feedback.
source: The fitting shows that the relationship between the proportion of contingent parental responses and the rate of transition from cries to phees can be explained by the development of the nervous system facilitated by parental feedback.
evidence: This is stated after fitting the model with the nervous system component to the data in Figure 6c.

claim: Infant marmoset monkeys with faster growth rates do not receive more contingent feedback from parents.
source: We find that no coefficient bi is significantly different from zero (n=10, b0=0.083p=0.675, p=0.675, b1=0.290, p=0.361, b2=−0.051 p=0.678).
evidence: This is demonstrated by statistical analysis showing no significant correlation between weight change and parental feedback.

claim: Parental feedback has a direct effect on the infant nervous system that cannot be accounted for by the growth or call rates of infants.
source: This corroborates the alternative hypothesis that parental feedback has a direct effect on the infant nervous system that cannot be accounted for by the growth or call rates of infants.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of correlation between infant growth/call rate and parental feedback.

claim: Development of vocal tract length L changes the resonance frequency by shifting the troughs/valleys of the landscape.
source: Development of vocal tract length L changes the resonance frequency by shifting the troughs/valleys of the landscape represented by the shape of gt⁢(θ) (Figure 8c)
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 8c showing how the landscape shifts with changes in L.

claim: Neuromuscular maturation increases the probability to produce phees by rotating the landscape.
source: neuromuscular maturation increases the probability to produce phees by reducing the cost function by an amount δ⁢θ per day, i.e. rotating the landscape from one postnatal day to the next (Figure 8d)
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 8d showing landscape rotation.

claim: Nervous system development driven by social feedback increases the probability to produce phees by tilting the entire landscape.
source: nervous system development driven by social feedback further increases the probability to produce phees by tilting the entire landscape by an amount that is the product of the learning rate κ and the proportion of parental feedback F (Figure 8e).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 8e showing landscape tilting.

claim: The biomechanical model is based on Titze's one-mass model of vocal fold dynamics.
source: The resulting biomechanical model of the larynx and upper vocal tract is based on the one-mass model of Titze (Titze, 1988), which is simpler than earlier two-mass models (Ishizaka and Flanagan, 1972; Herzel, 1993; Lucero, 1993) and can produce a wide range of birdsong (Amador and Mindlin, 2008; Perl et al., 2011; Amador et al., 2013).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with citations to the relevant literature.

claim: The model assumes bilateral symmetry in vocal fold oscillations.
source: Bilateral symmetry in vocal fold oscillations is assumed, simplifying the system to a single degree of freedom oscillator
evidence: This is a stated assumption of the model.

claim: The model uses source-filter theory which assumes that vocal fold dynamics are independent of filtering within the upper vocal tract.
source: Again seeking simplicity, we appeal to source-filter theory, which assumes that the vocal fold dynamics are independent of filtering within the upper vocal tract (Titze, 1994).
evidence: This is a stated assumption supported by citation to Titze, 1994.

claim: The upper vocal tract is modeled as a uniform cylinder.
source: The resulting pressure changes propagate through the upper vocal tract and mouth cavity, which we model as a uniform cylinder.
evidence: This is an explicit statement of the modeling approach.

claim: The origin of cries in the model is due to a mismatch between low frequency periodic glottal air flow and the higher frequency resonance of the infant's upper vocal tract.
source: Our model produces cries simply through a mismatch between the low frequency periodic glottal air flow and the higher frequency resonance of the infant's upper vocal tract; no chaotic dynamics occurs.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the model that contrasts with previous hypotheses.

claim: The primary difference between cries and phee calls is that the frequency of glottal oscillations is lower in cries.
source: The primary difference between cries and phee calls is that the frequency of glottal oscillations is lower in the former (see Figure 9 (left)).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 9.

claim: Cries are the scaffolding for vocal maturation in both marmosets and humans.
source: This result provides direct biomechanical support for the hypothesis that cries are the scaffolding for vocal maturation in both marmosets (Takahashi et al., 2015) and humans (Kent and Murray, 1982).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion supported by the model results and citations.

claim: All experiments were approved by the Princeton University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.
source: All experiments were approved by the Princeton University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.
evidence: This is an explicit statement of ethical approval.

claim: Vocalizations were recorded in two contexts: undirected (social isolation) and directed (with auditory contact with a parent).
source: The vocalizations of marmoset monkey infants were recorded starting on the first postnatal day in two different contexts: undirected (i.e., social isolation) and directed (with auditory, but not visual, contact with their mother or father).
evidence: This is stated in the experimental procedures section.

claim: Audio signals were acquired at a sampling frequency of 96 kHz.
source: Audio signals were acquired at a sampling frequency of 96 kHz.
evidence: This is a methodological detail stated in the experimental procedures.

claim: The zero-crossing day is defined as the first point at which the phee/cry ratio curve crossed zero, transitioning from negative to positive.
source: The zero-crossing day was defined as the first point at which the phee/cry ratio curve crossed zero, transitioning from a negative to a positive value.
evidence: This is a methodological definition stated in the methods.

claim: A parental call was classified as contingent if it occurred within 5 s of an infant call offset with no other call between them.
source: A parental call was classified as a contingent response to an infant call if the parental call onset was separated by less than 5 s from the infant call offset with no other call between them (Takahashi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a methodological definition with citation support.

claim: The learning parameter κ was estimated to be 0.2126.
source: Fitting the function to the data relating the amount of parental feedback (F) and zero-crossing day z0, we get κ=0.2126 and δ=0.0654.
evidence: This is a parameter value obtained from fitting the model to data.

claim: The neuromuscular maturation parameter δ was estimated to be 0.0654.
source: Fitting the function to the data relating the amount of parental feedback (F) and zero-crossing day z0, we get κ=0.2126 and δ=0.0654.
evidence: This is a parameter value obtained from fitting the model to data.

claim: The classification of call types matched in more than 99.9% of cases between two independent classifiers.
source: To ensure validity of our classification procedure, 10 sessions chosen at random were classified by two different individuals and compared. The classification matched in more than 99.9% of the call syllables.
evidence: This is a validation result stated in the methods.

claim: Parental call rate and strength of dynamic interaction between infants and parents remain constant throughout development.
source: The behavioral data do not support this alternative sequence of events: parental call rate, and strength of the dynamic interaction between infants and parents, remain constant throughout development (Takahashi et al., 2015, 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citation support to justify the inferential sequence used.

claim: Infants who do not vocalize much tend to be fed and held less by mothers and are slowed in their vocal development.
source: Infants who do not vocalize much tend to be fed and held less by mothers, and are slowed in their vocal development.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as background on infant vocal development.

claim: Recent innovations have established genetically-modified marmosets.
source: Recent innovations establishing genetically-modified marmosets (Sasaki et al., 2009; Okano et al., 2016) will allow for any number of experimental routes needed to gain novel insights into vocal development.
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Squirrel monkey vocalizations change very little during development.
source: For instance, the landscapes of New World squirrel monkeys, whose vocalizations change very little during development (Hammerschmidt et al., 2001), could be quantitatively compared to each other and with the marmoset landscape.
evidence: This is stated with citation support as a comparative example.

claim: The Bengalese finch is a domesticated counterpart of the white-rumped munia.
source: Similarly, evolutionary insights could be gained by comparing vocal development landscapes of the white-rumped munia and its domesticated counterpart, the Bengalese finch, whose song behaviors and biologies differ considerably (Katahira et al., 2013; Suzuki et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: The dataset analyzed in this work was previously published by Takahashi et al., 2015.
source: The data analyzed in this work is a subset of the dataset that was previously published (Takahashi et al., 2015) and can be found at http://science.sciencemag.org/content/suppl/2015/08/13/349.6249.734.DC1.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the methods section.

claim: The colony room was maintained at approximately 27°C and 50-60% relative humidity with a 12L:12D light cycle.
source: The colony room is maintained at a temperature of approximately 27°C and 50–60% relative humidity, with a 12L:12D light cycle.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about housing conditions.

claim: Pink noise was broadcast at 45 dB to mask occasional external noises during experiments.
source: A speaker was placed at a third corner equidistant from both testing corners and pink noise (amplitude decaying inversely proportional to frequency) was broadcast at 45 dB (at 0.88 m from speaker) in order to mask occasional noises produced external to the testing room.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about experimental procedures.

claim: Undirected experiments lasted 5 minutes each.
source: Each session started with the undirected experiments lasting 5 min each.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about experimental duration.

claim: The total number of undirected experiments with at least one call production was 301 sessions across 10 infants.
source: The number of undirected experiments with at least one call production was 40, 38, 38, 38, 37, 39, 19, 15, 16, 21 (10 infants, 301 sessions, 73,421 utterances).
evidence: This is a summary of the dataset used in the study.

claim: The total number of directed experiments was 195 sessions across 10 infants.
source: The number of directed experiments for each infant was 17, 13, 13, 18, 24, 24, 22, 21, 21, 22 (10 infants, 195 sessions).
evidence: This is a summary of the dataset used in the study.

claim: A total of 73,421 utterances were analyzed in the undirected context.
source: The number of undirected experiments with at least one call production was 40, 38, 38, 38, 37, 39, 19, 15, 16, 21 (10 infants, 301 sessions, 73,421 utterances).
evidence: This is stated as part of the dataset description.

claim: The 99th percentile of the amplitude value in silent periods was used as the detection threshold for vocalizations.
source: The 99th percentile of the amplitude value in the silent period was used as the detection threshold.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about call detection.

claim: A whole call was defined as any uninterrupted sequence of utterances of the same type with inter-utterance intervals less than 500 ms.
source: For the directed calls experiments, a whole (i.e., multisyllabic) call was defined as any uninterrupted sequence of utterances of the same type (phee or cry) with previous offset to next onset separated by less than 500 ms (DiMattina and Wang, 2006; Takahashi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a methodological definition with citation support.

claim: The time constant γ was set to 45 (1/ms) in the model.
source: γ	Time constant (1/ms)	45
evidence: This is stated in Table 1 of parameter values.

claim: The reflection coefficient r was set to 0.8 in the model.
source: r	Pressure reflection coefficient	0.8
evidence: This is stated in Table 1 of parameter values.

claim: The one-way sound travel time in the vocal tract (T/2) was set to 50 μs in the model.
source: T/2	Time for one way sound travel in vocal tract (μs)	50
evidence: This is stated in Table 1 of parameter values.

claim: Numerical simulations used a time step size of 5 μs.
source: d⁢t	Time step size (μs)	5
evidence: This is stated in Table 1 of parameter values.

claim: The pressure coefficient c was set to 1 in the model.
source: c	Pressure coefficient	1
evidence: This is stated in Table 1 of parameter values.

claim: Euler's method was used for numerical simulations of the vocal fold equations.
source: Numerical simulations of Equations (14) and (16–17) were carried out using Euler's method in custom written MATLAB codes.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: Pink noise was added to model simulations to match background noise in real recordings.
source: To improve the fit between the model and recordings, pink noise was added to the simulation to match its presence in the background of the exemplar vocalizations in Figure 3b–e
evidence: This is stated in the methods describing simulation procedures.

claim: Only in region I of the parameter space do robust stable limit cycles and hence calls exist.
source: Only in the shaded region I, lying above the upper saddle-node bifurcation curve and to the right of the Hopf bifurcation curve, do robust stable limit cycles and hence calls exist, to which almost all solutions converge.
evidence: This is stated in the analysis of the model dynamics and shown in Figure 10.

claim: Each passage around the limit cycle corresponds to the vocal folds opening and closing once.
source: Each passage around the cycle corresponds to the vocal folds opening and closing once.
evidence: This is stated in the interpretation of the model dynamics.

claim: Vocalizations are produced at approximately once per second in infant marmosets.
source: If vocalizations are produced at periodic intervals (approximately once per second in infant marmosets [Zhang and Ghazanfar, 2016])
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: The model does not include chaotic dynamics to produce cries.
source: Our model produces cries simply through a mismatch between the low frequency periodic glottal air flow and the higher frequency resonance of the infant's upper vocal tract; no chaotic dynamics occurs.
evidence: This is stated as a contrast with previous models.

claim: Previous models attributed cries to turbulent or chaotic dynamics of the vocal folds.
source: For example, the origin of cries in nonhuman primates has been attributed to turbulent or chaotic dynamics of the vocal folds (Fitch et al., 2002), perhaps as a consequence of vocal fold asymmetry (Herzel, 1993) and/or source-vocal tract interactions (Hatzikirou et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citations as background on previous models.

claim: The model does not separately model the mouth cavity.
source: Unlike the zebra finch song model of Amador et al. (Amador et al., 2013), we do not model the mouth cavity separately; our model can reproduce typical marmoset calls well without this refinement
evidence: This is stated as a simplification in the model.

claim: The model parameters were fit manually to match spectrotemporal data of calls.
source: To verify that the model could reproduce realistic marmoset calls, the parameters were fit manually to match the spectrotemporal data of calls as shown in Figure 3b–e.
evidence: This is stated in the methods describing parameter fitting.

claim: The vocal development landscape framework can be used to make quantitative predictions regarding experimental perturbations.
source: We can thus use this framework to make quantitative predictions regarding how interfering factors or experimental perturbations can change the landscape within a species, or to explain comparative differences in vocal development across species
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a potential application of the framework.

claim: The landscape framework could be used to make predictions regarding influences of communication-related genes expressed during neuroembryological development.
source: For example, the landscape framework combined with genetic engineering could be used to make predictions regarding the influences of communication- or connectivity-related genes expressed during neuroembryological development in marmosets (Matsunaga et al., 2013; Kato et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as a potential future application with citation support.

claim: The vocal development landscape may be used to illuminate why there are species differences in the degree to which vocalizations can be learned.
source: The vocal development landscape may be used to illuminate why there are species differences in both the degree to which vocalizations can be learned and the life history-timing of such learning.
evidence: This is stated as a potential application of the framework.

claim: Providing developmental parameters for different species could illuminate how changes in their landscapes lead to similarities or differences in adult vocal behaviors.
source: Moreover, as the evolution of a phenotype in essence defines its developmental trajectory, providing the developmental parameters for different species could illuminate how changes in their respective landscapes lead to similarities or differences in their adult vocal behaviors.
evidence: This is stated as a potential evolutionary application of the framework.

claim: The integrated systems view provided by the vocal development landscape eschews the view that there are privileged levels of understanding behavior.
source: Overall, we believe that the integrated systems view provided by the vocal development landscape not only eschews the incorrect view that there are privileged levels of understanding behavior and its development (Noble, 2012; Krakauer et al., 2017)
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation support.

claim: The framework enables predictions of how natural or experimental perturbations will affect vocal behavior development.
source: but also enables us to make predictions regarding how natural or experimental perturbations (e.g., changes in social feedback, weakening of muscles, disruptions of neural circuits, genetic engineering, etc.) will affect the development of vocal behavior, and why species differ in their capacity to learn communication signals.
evidence: This is stated as a benefit of the framework in the discussion.
